drafts.title: Tactile temperature and fan controls operable without looking
drafts.description: When driving, the driver can adjust cabin temperature and fan speed by touch only (no visual confirmation required) using distinct, tactile controls that are reachable from the driving position.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In a driving user test, 95% of participants can (a) change cabin temperature by at least 2 °C and (b) change fan speed by one level using only touch (no glance) within 3 seconds per action.
assumptions: Temperature resolution of 1–2 °C is meaningful to users and used in the test.
Controls are within ergonomic reach and positioned similarly to today's 5 Series layout.
Test participants represent typical US drivers (mixed hand sizes, some wearing sunglasses; glove tests handled separately).
uncertainties: Exact tactile design and placement that deliver the required recognition time may need iterative user testing.
Glove use (heavy winter gloves) may reduce tactile discriminability and require additional design work.

drafts.title: Reliable natural-language voice control for common driving tasks
drafts.description: Drivers can use voice to perform common driving tasks (navigation destinations, media/playback, phone calls, basic climate commands) while driving and expect consistent, correct execution without repeated attempts.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Under realistic driving noise (city and highway) tests using a standardized set of 50 common commands, the system correctly executes 95% of commands within 3 seconds and requires no repeat attempt in more than 90% of failures.
assumptions: Tests include a representative mix of US accents and ambient vehicle noise profiles.
Cloud assistance may be used where allowed; on-device fallback is available for basic commands when connectivity is degraded.
uncertainties: Privacy restrictions or regional cloud limitations may affect performance in some markets.
Long-tail accents or non-standard phrasing may require additional language model training post-launch.

drafts.title: Consistent wireless phone charging across popular phones
drafts.description: When a compatible phone is placed on the vehicle wireless charging pad, charging reliably starts and continues throughout typical trips without unexpected disconnects.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In bench and in-vehicle tests, the wireless pad successfully starts and maintains charging for at least 95% of placement attempts across the top 20 US phone models by sales during a continuous 30-minute driving session, and automatically recovers charging after brief phone movement or repositioning.
assumptions: Top 20 phone models are defined by US sales data at vehicle launch.
Tests include phones with commonly used thin cases (up to ~3 mm).
Test sessions represent typical driving dynamics (bumpy roads, turns).
uncertainties: Future phone designs (new form factors, magnetic attachments) may affect compatibility after launch.
Some proprietary phone models may require firmware or alignment changes outside vehicle scope.

drafts.title: Readable head‑up display and center screen in bright sunlight
drafts.description: Critical driving and navigation information shown in the HUD and primary center screen remains legible to drivers in bright sunlight, including when wearing sunglasses.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In outdoor tests at midday sunlight (>50,000 lux), 90% of test participants (including those wearing sunglasses) can correctly read critical HUD indicators and primary center‑screen navigation/driving info within 1.5 seconds.
assumptions: Midday sunlight test level is approximated at >50,000 lux to represent challenging but common conditions.
Participants include users wearing common sunglasses (polarized and non-polarized).
HUD brightness and center screen brightness are adjustable within allowed regulatory limits.
uncertainties: Extreme reflective interiors or aftermarket window tints may still cause localized readability issues.
Trade-offs between screen brightness (legibility) and night-time glare need verification.

drafts.title: Heated steering wheel included by default in Cold Weather package
drafts.description: In markets where a Cold Weather (or equivalent) package is offered, the heated steering wheel is included in that package so customers do not have to buy it as a costly standalone option.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: In the US configurator and dealer ordering system the Cold Weather package includes the heated steering wheel as standard; at least 95% of Cold Weather package orders recorded over the first 12 months include the heated steering wheel as part of that package.
assumptions: Package naming and composition is harmonized in the US market configurator and dealer order-entry systems.
Dealers honor configured package contents when placing orders.
uncertainties: Regional market variations or legacy order systems may delay full rollout in some channels.
If hardware variants differ between trim levels, inclusion may require minor hardware alignment.

drafts.title: Allow heated seats to be activated via an in-vehicle digital subscription toggle
drafts.description: Customers can enable heated seats from the vehicle UI or companion app via a digital activation (subscription), without needing a dealer visit, and the feature becomes usable shortly after activation.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Users can subscribe and enable heated seats from the vehicle UI or companion app and have the function activated within 5 minutes; 95% of activation attempts succeed and the activation persists across vehicle power cycles for at least 30 days.
assumptions: Heated-seats hardware is physically present in vehicles but may be software-locked for subscription activation.
A cloud/backend commerce platform and payment integration are available at launch in the target market(s).
Regional commerce regulations and app-store/payment provider approvals are obtained where required.
uncertainties: Payment provider integration timelines and regional restrictions may delay full availability in some regions.
Customer acceptance of subscription model varies; pricing is out of scope and handled by commercial teams.

drafts.title: China CCC certification request (regulatory request — out of scope for product requirements)
drafts.description: Customers asked that the infotainment system pass CCC certification for the Chinese market. Certification and homologation activities are legal/regulatory workstreams outside the product-level customer-experience requirements.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Out of scope for product feature requirements; handled by regulatory/homologation teams per regional compliance processes.
assumptions: Regulatory certification processes are managed by legal and compliance organizations.
Product may need minor adaptations to meet specific region rules; those are tracked separately.
uncertainties: Certification timelines and local technical requirements may affect launch timing in China.
drafts.scope_reason: Regulation/homologation request handled by compliance teams, not a customer-facing product requirement.

drafts.title: GDPR compliance request for driver profile (legal/data-protection — out of scope for product-level requirements)
drafts.description: Customers asked that the driver profile satisfy every GDPR requirement for data storage. GDPR compliance is a legal/data-protection obligation and is handled by legal/IT/compliance teams rather than as a product feature requirement.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Out of scope for product requirement drafts; data-protection and legal compliance are tracked and validated by the company’s privacy and compliance functions.
assumptions: Privacy teams will define technical controls and user data rights (export/delete) as required by law.
Product teams will implement interfaces for user data controls as specified by privacy policies (if needed).
uncertainties: Interpretation of GDPR requirements for new features (e.g., subscriptions, profiles) may require product changes once legal defines controls.
drafts.scope_reason: Legal/regulatory compliance (GDPR) is not a product feature requirement but a compliance activity.

drafts.title: Request for a specific cockpit chip (engineering specification — out of scope)
drafts.description: Customers requested the cockpit computer to use the Snapdragon 8295 chip. Specific component choices are engineering specifications and outside customer-facing requirement scope.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Out of scope for customer-facing requirement drafts; chipset selection is an engineering decision evaluated for performance, cost, and supplier constraints.
assumptions: Engineering and procurement will select hardware based on performance, availability and cost targets.
Customer-facing outcomes (e.g., responsiveness) should be specified instead of specific chip names.
uncertainties: Supply chain availability and obsolescence may require alternative chip choices.
drafts.scope_reason: Specific part/chip request is an engineering specification and therefore out of scope for customer-facing requirements.

drafts.title: Requests to lower base price, change lease/finance pricing, or make packages free (commercial/pricing — out of scope)
drafts.description: Customers requested a base price below $50,000, cheaper monthly leases vs. competitors, 0% financing, free option packages, or specific package discounts. Pricing, financing and dealer margin policy are commercial decisions outside product requirement scope.
drafts.acceptance_criterion: Out of scope for product requirement drafts; pricing, lease and financing programs are handled by commercial/finance teams.
assumptions: Commercial, finance and regional sales teams own pricing, dealer margin and financing programs.
Product teams will provide package composition and feature availability; pricing is defined by separate stakeholders.
uncertainties: Market dynamics and competitive actions may prompt future commercial offers that affect feature uptake.
drafts.scope_reason: Price, lease, financing and dealer-margin requests are commercial decisions outside the scope of product feature requirements.
